original.target_description: Within-participant comparison of Transportation Scale scores after literary fiction versus nonfiction, final undergraduate sample; paired t test.

n.location: p. 34, section 1.1 Participants; p. 36, section 2.1 (paired-test df 59)
n.quote: The ﬁnal sample consisted of 60 students
n.sample_role: Participants contributing paired fiction/nonfiction transportation scores.
n.exclusions: 91 completed; excluded cases with reading time below mean minus 1.5 SD on any text or RME time below mean minus 2 SD.

replication.target_description: One-way ANOVA of narrative transportation across challenging fiction, easy fiction, and nonfiction; final MTurk sample. This is the omnibus test of reading condition, rather than a pooled fiction-versus-nonfiction contrast.

n.location: p. 424, Method, Participants; p. 426, Results (ANOVA df 2, 891)
n.quote: Participants (n = 111) were excluded if they did not give at least 60% correct responses to the attention check questions; final sample greater than our proposed power analysis suggested (N final = 894).
n.sample_role: Final participants across all three conditions in the transportation ANOVA; challenging fiction 296, easy fiction 300, nonfiction 298.
n.exclusions: 1005 recruited; 111 excluded for attention-check accuracy below 60%. 218 reporting prior exposure retained because their inclusion did not change significance decisions.

reported_success.quote: Although these results did not replicate Black and Barnes’ (2015a) finding that literary fiction engenders higher narrative transportation than nonfiction

notes: Titles and DOI strings verified in both retrieved full papers. Input has no study-specific locators; selected tests directly addressing its neutral description, reading material and transportation. Replication reports an omnibus three-condition test with printed partial eta squared, retained without conversion to requested d. Its post hoc challenging-fiction versus nonfiction comparison has p > .99 but no accompanying printed effect size; it is not combined with the omnibus effect size. Authors’ failure verdict concerns the original directional fiction-versus-nonfiction finding despite the significant omnibus condition test.
